# ForeSight RPG
<!--{ "pin": "top", "order": 0, "headTitle": "ForeSight RPG — a streamlined tabletop RPG", "description": "A modern edition of the ForeSight RPG: one resolution rule (Score × Ease Factor), lethal fast combat, and a careful generative magic system." }-->

A streamlined, modern edition of the **ForeSight** tabletop RPG, built on the unpublished 2004 second edition and the 1986 original.

**One rule:** Success Chance = Score × Ease Factor — roll D100 under it. Everything else is that rule applied to different situations.

Use the navigation to browse the rules one-pagers, or open the live **[Character Builder](/character-builder/)**.

## This is work-in-progress

If you have a problem with these rules [file an issue](https://github.com/tonioloewald/foresight-rpg/issues). But remember, the goal of ForeSight is to be "all the rules you can remember", so producing big lists of stuff or complex definitive procedures for things (like Aftermath's bullet impact resolution flowchart, or Universe's wilderness encounter system, or even RuneQuest 3's Dropped Oil Lamp Table) is not the point.

You, the GM or player, have better insight into the weird special case at hand than I or any game designer can ever possibly have. Use [the one rule](/the-one-rule/) and get on with the game.

## Colophon

This site, the "app" you're using, the system that turns it into a printable page or an ePub, was all created using the [tosijs documentation system](https://ui.tosijs.net/one-source-every-artifact/) which itself is one of the end results of a forty-year career building software that was started because I wanted to publish **these rules**.

# Magic
<!--{ "pin": "top", "order": 4 }-->

*ForeSight's magic — descended from **HindSight & the Age of Reason** (1987) — is **generative**: you don't pick a spell off a list, you **compose** an effect from the **Applications** of one or more **Fundamentals**. It is versatile to the point of danger, which is why the first rule of magic isn't a rule at all — it's a decision the **GM** makes about the world.*

## First, decide what magic *is* in this world

Magic shapes a setting more than any other system, so ForeSight's transparency principle bites hardest here: magic's reach must be an **explicit choice, never an accident**. Before anyone casts anything, the GM sets three dials:

| Dial | The question | Runs from… |
|---|---|---|
| **Common** | Who can do it? | no one · a rare few · commonplace |
| **Powerful** | How far does it reach? | parlour tricks · real force · world-shaking |
| **Prominent** | Does the world *know*? | hidden/feared/illegal · an open, ordinary craft |

These compose into the setting's **Magic level** (the character sheet's magic axis: *none · rare-weak · rare · common-weak · common*), and they change the world, not just the rules. A setting where a **reliable truth-spell** exists is a *different world* — its courts, its spies, its secrets all work differently. Decide that on purpose.

## How casting works — gather, then weave

Magic runs on **two skills**, and the split is the whole engine:

- **Mana** — you **gather** the energy an effect needs. This is the roll that meters cost: it's the [Exhaustion](/exhaustion/) gather-roll, so reaching for a firestorm in a mana-poor place is simply more exhausting than a candle-flame in a mana-rich one.
- **Incantation** — you **weave** the gathered energy into the effect. Its difficulty tracks the effect's **complexity**, *not* its size.

**Complexity and energy are separate axes.** A big, simple effect (a wall of flame) is *energy*-hungry — that's what **rituals** buy: time traded for the power to gather more. A small, intricate effect (a subtle, conditional glamour) is *complexity*-hungry — that's a hard weave no amount of ritual makes trivial. **Snap-casting** is the reverse trade: speed bought with a harsh ease-factor penalty.

## Effects are composed from Fundamentals

A **Fundamental** is a *Field of Magical Knowledge* (so it obeys the [Fields](/fields/) rules — **Basic** covers the easy end, **Advanced** the deep). Each Fundamental offers a set of **Applications**, each rated by an **Intensity** (its difficulty and mana flux). A **Magical Effect** is one core application plus any number of **modifiers** — a *spell* and its *metaspells* — assembled just like modifying any other object in ForeSight. An effect is only ever as good as its meanest part: its **range and duration are the smallest** of its components'. The GM adjudicates whether the combination actually produces the intended effect.

There are **23 Fundamentals**, each with its own page and its applications laid out as a table and cards (browse them below) — or, if you know the effect you want but not where it lives, **[find any effect](/magic-find/)** by name or description across all of them.

## Keeping it balanced — the keystones

Because the system is generative, balance can't live in a spell list; it lives in a handful of principles the GM applies to any effect a player invents:

- **Conscious targets resist direct magic.** An unwilling or unaware mind *intrinsically* resists a spell aimed at it — magic gets no free pass on people, which is what keeps "I charm the king" from ending campaigns.
- **Coercion is never cheaper than consent.** Bending someone against their will always costs more than the same thing done with their agreement.
- **Bestowal is gated per effect** — whether an effect is *controlled* (you steer it live), *bestowed* (handed to a target or item), *fixed*, or *immediate* is priced separately, because a fire you throw once and a fire you *grant* someone forever are not the same purchase.
- **Benchmark against the mundane.** Judge an effect against what a skilled person does *without* magic — in combat, a good archer; socially, ask what the world becomes if the effect is **reliable** (a reliable truth-detector is transformative, and priced as such).
- **Price the capability, not its costume.** Two effects that accomplish the same thing cost the same, however differently they're dressed.

*Designer's Note: the point of a generative system is that players surprise you — four playtesters once found four different ways to conjure an instant fortress in about two minutes. That's a feature, but only if the GM prices the **capability** rather than the flavour, and only if magic can't quietly do to the setting what the GM never agreed to. Everything above exists to keep "you can build anything" from becoming "so nothing matters."*

# ForeSight 1986
<!--{ "pin": "top", "order": 99, "book": "foresight-1986", "headTitle": "ForeSight 1986 — the original edition (restoration in progress)", "description": "A community restoration of the original 1986 ForeSight rules — machine-extracted from the first edition with the 1987 errata folded in. Work in progress; corrections welcome." }-->

> **⚠️ Work in progress — a machine restoration, not a clean text (yet).**
> These pages are **automatically extracted** from the original 1986 first edition
> and still carry OCR noise — garbled table cells, stray characters, the odd
> run-together line. They are published *because* they're rough: help us finish
> restoring them.

*This is the **original ForeSight** (Tonio Loewald, 1986, ISBN 0958789401) — the edition that actually shipped and was **playtested hard for years**. In all that time, no errors turned up beyond the single [1987 errata sheet](#the-1987-errata), which is folded in below. That track record is why the 1986 numbers are treated as **calibration ground-truth** for the modern edition: where the streamlined rules and the original disagree on a probability, the original has the table evidence.*

## Why it's here

The out-of-print 1986 rules are hard to find, and a number of players want a faithful, readable copy very badly. So rather than sit on a private extraction, it's public — rough edges and all — as a base the community can correct toward a fully-restored original.

## How the extraction works (so you can read around the noise)

- **Prose** is reflowed into normal paragraphs and lightly de-noised (only unambiguous OCR fixes — nothing is reworded, and no rule is "improved").
- **Tables and stat charts** (the Master Weapon Chart, vehicle and starship tables) are shown **verbatim in monospaced blocks** to preserve their alignment. These are the noisiest part and the most valuable to clean up.
- Each page carries an invisible `<!-- 1986 p.N -->` marker (view source) so a correction can cite the original page.
- This section is **site-only** — it's deliberately left out of the streamlined edition's ePub; it's a different book.

## Help finish it

Corrections are hugely welcome — this is exactly the kind of thing a few dozen readers can fix faster than one person. Spot a mangled table cell, a dropped word, a chart that needs rebuilding?

- **File an issue or a pull request** on the repo: **[github.com/tonioloewald/foresight-rpg](https://github.com/tonioloewald/foresight-rpg)** — cite the page number from the source marker.
- The source lives in `src/rules/1986-*.md`; table blocks are the priority.

## The 1987 errata

The only known corrections to the 1986 rules, printed **Fri, Oct 23 1987**, keyed to the book's chapter-page codes (`2xx` Characters, `3xx` Resolution, `5xx` Travel, `7xx` Star System, `8xx` Starships):

- **Skills / Limit (205R)** — *"1 indicates a skill where talent is as important as experience; 1.5 indicates a skill where experience outweighs talent. A character may not possess a skill at a level higher than the highest of the attributes … in the skill's formula, multiplied by its limit, plus two (rounded off)."* (The headline fix; already present in this printing.)
- **Resolution table (facing 301)** — the "30" row / "QR4" column entry should be **30**.
- **Travel (501R)** — the terrain-value limit for **submarine** vehicles should be **2**.
- **Travel (502L)** — the net **Red(line)** rating is normal Red **plus** (Modified Terrain Value)/2 *(still misprinted as "minus" — see the inline note on the Travel page)*; and *"(or 1 if this is lower)"* means divide by one only if the **result** would be lower.
- **Pursuit (504L)** — "double back" is the old name for the **reverse** manoeuvre.
- **Star System (703R)** — the Incident Radiation Table's bottom row was displaced; a corrected table + collected modifiers were issued.
- **Starships (804R)** — Hibersleep compartments **do not consume 0.25 power**; they run on bleed power from the drives.

# Equipment
<!--{ "parent": "world", "order": 1 }-->

*One-pager — the keystone. Everything you can own, drive, wield, or wear is an **object**: a basic object (a noun) plus modifications (adjectives). Weapons, armor, vehicles, and tools are just objects with extra stats. NPCs and monsters use the same pattern (see those pages).*

## Object = noun + adjectives

A **basic object** is the noun: *sword*, *pistol*, *sedan*, *backpack*. A **modification** is an adjective with a defined game effect: *fine*, *shoddy*, *sporty*, *cut-down*. You build the item you want by putting adjectives in front of the noun — and that's exactly how you say it at the table: a *cut-down pistol*, a *sporty sedan*.

This is also how the catalog stays short. If a "new" item is really a variant of one you already have, it isn't a separate entry — it's an adjective on an existing noun: a **carbine** is a *light rifle*, a **destrier** is a *warhorse*. One good adjective often covers several real items: the weapon-specific **cut-down** gives you both a sawn-off shotgun *and* a snub-nose revolver — easier to conceal, worse at range. One noun, many items.

## Stats every object can have

Most objects need only a couple of these; list a stat only when it isn't obvious.

| Stat | What it is |
|---|---|
| **PM** (Performance Modifier) | the ease-factor modifier for using the object as intended — a *+1* sword is a better sword, but does nothing extra hammering nails. Some objects carry several labeled PMs (a melee weapon has Attack, Parry, Damage) |
| **Size / Weight** | for carrying, concealment, and encumbrance |
| **TL** | its technology level — whether a culture can buy, repair, or *originate* it (see [Technology Levels](/technology-levels/)) |
| **Price** | in svu |
| **Fail** | how prone it is to break or jam, if that ever matters |
| **Damage Scale** | for very large or tough objects (see [Damage](/damage/)) |

## Categories

Each category is its own short, **alphabetized** list with a few category-specific stats:

| Category | Its stats |
|---|---|
| **Weapons** | Attack, Parry, Damage (with type and penetration), Reach or Range, Usage (one/two-handed…) |
| **Armor** | Protection (by damage type), and the penalties it imposes (perception in a helmet, coordination in gauntlets, agility in a heavy suit) |
| **Vehicles** | Cruise, Max, Terrain, Accelerate, Turn, Redline, Passengers, Cargo. **Spacecraft are vehicles**; an electric/hybrid drive is a TL6 modification, not a new category |
| **Tools** | the PM they grant to the task they're for (binoculars, lock picks, a surgeon's kit) |
| **Other Stuff** | everything else, with the minimal stats it actually needs |

## Modifications (the general set)

These apply to almost anything; categories add their own.

| Mod | Effect |
|---|---|
| **Custom / Quality** | Pay a lot for one specific advantage (+1), often with a minor offset — usually reliability or weight. This is also what a character's own skill produces when they customize gear: a successful craft/tune task *makes* something Custom. |
| **Cheap / Shoddy** | Worse across the board, and especially unreliable — but much cheaper. |
| **Poorly Maintained** | Even more unreliable than Shoddy, and sometimes worse in other respects. A condition, not a price point; gear drifts here through neglect. |
| **Reliable** | Fails far less often. More expensive. |
| **Light** | Smaller, lighter, often cheaper — but a little worse, or lower capacity. |
| **Heavy** | Bigger, heavier, more expensive — higher capacity or sturdier. |

> **Grain note.** ForeSight's modifiers are **ease factors** — steps on the EF ladder (0, ¼, ½, 1, 2 … 15), applied before SC = Score × EF. A single step is a powerful lever: **+1 EF adds your whole Score to the success chance in the sweet spot** (Score 15 at EF 5→6 goes 75% → 90%, i.e. +15), and about **half your Score** down at the ¼/½ rungs. (Contrast ForePlay, where +1 was a flat ~10%, tapering at the edges.) Two consequences: modifiers stay small — a modification is usually just **±1 EF** — and the same +1 helps a more skilled character *more* in absolute terms. When porting ForePlay numbers, **its +2 or +3 maps to roughly +1 EF here**, never one-to-one.

## Descriptions: say what it is and why you'd want one

List entries get **minimal** descriptions — but useful ones. The job of a description is to tell a reader what the thing *is* and *why a character would carry it*. D&D famously listed a 10′ pole and never said it was for probing floors for traps from a safe distance; don't do that. One honest sentence beats a paragraph of stats restated in prose.

*Designer's Note: "objects are nouns plus adjectives" is the same idea that runs through NPCs, vehicles, and even background factors. Learn it once and the whole back half of the book is the same move applied to different lists. (And you already speak this language — nobody says "pistol, cut-down"; they say "cut-down pistol.")*

# ForeSight — GM Cheat Sheet
<!--{ "parent": "reference", "order": 1 }-->

## The One Rule

> **Success Chance = Score × Ease Factor.** Roll **D100 ≤ SC** to succeed.

**EF ladder:** 0 — ¼ — ½ — 1 — 2 — 3 … 15. (0 = impossible, 15 = automatic.) Add all modifiers, *then* apply.

**A +1 EF is worth your whole Score** in the sweet spot (Score 15: EF 5→6 = 75%→90%), ~half at the ¼/½ rungs. Keep modifiers small.

**Rule of thumb:** `+5` trivial · `+3` very easy · `+1` easy · `0` average · `−1` hard · `−3` very hard · `−5` extreme · `−7` near-impossible. *(Just remember +5 easy / −5 hard.)*

## Quality Ratings

| Roll vs SC | QR |
|---|---|
| ≤ SC/10 | **QR1** |
| ≤ SC/4 | **QR2** |
| ≤ SC/2 | **QR3** |
| ≤ SC | **QR4** |
| > SC | **QR7** (fail) |
| > SC & a multiple of 10 | **QR10** (botch) |

*Caps: a 100 is never better than QR7; a 99 never better than QR4.*

**Yield %:** QR1 **100** · QR2 **80** · QR3 **50** · QR4 **25** (failures yield as QR4).
**Read one column only:** *Yield* (how much) · *Time* (QR4 ≈ 200% of estimate) · *PM* = **4 − QR**. Never penalize the same choice twice (pay the EF up front, the success includes it).

## Open-Ended Resolution

- **Oppose:** both roll, **compare QRs** — better wins; **equal cancels** (just-barely block; keep going); break ties by Score only if forced.
- **Block (how much got through):** defense ≥ attack negates; else attack drops **(5 − defending QR)** notches; failed defense = full; QR10 defense = attack one notch *worse*.
- **Build on a result:** **+(5 − QR)** as an EF *modifier* (QR1 +4 … QR4 +1); opposing a standing result, same as a penalty.

## Damage

> **Damage = Yield × (DC ÷ 2)** ⟶ wound levels.  (Large/tough target: **÷ Damage Scale**.)

**DC anchors:** inhumanly-strong fist **4** · 9mm pistol **8** · 7.62 rifle **11**.
**Types:** M melee · I impact · B beam. **P**n weapon pierces n DC of armor; armor **A** absorbs 1 damage.
**Hit location:** roll D10, or call the shot for an up-front EF penalty (covers cover, too).

## Combat (sequence)

1. **Awareness → Initiative.** Surprised → Startled → Alert → Ready → Lying-in-wait; modify for big factors (can't see = bad). Sets the roll.
2. **Declare best → worst Init** (ties by Score): each chooses **Act** or **Wait**. Waiting *persists* across rounds — the unaware get no declaration turn 1 (ambush!).
3. **React / pre-empt:** a waiter reacting may go just after — or **pre-empt** (Coordination roll modified by Initiative QR, ties by Init Score) to go just before. *Nobody is ever certain they act first.*
4. **Your turn:** one **Primary** + one **Secondary** action (no AP budget; throughput = skill & body).
5. **Reactions** (parry/dodge/flinch/cover): unlimited, **cumulative −2 each**.

*Round ≈ 3–5 s (longer for vehicles). Spread attacks — a hurt/stunned foe is far less dangerous than a dead-or-healthy one.*

## Wounds, Stun & Exhaustion

**Wound level** 0→8(dead); **−(level) to everything**. New damage adds on. Pain Resistance (EN *or* WP) on a hit → shrug / **Shaken** (−2, one action) / **Stunned** (only recover-from-stun; QR1 clears, QR10 KO).
**Convalescence:** roll EN/WP at the level's interval (Light daily, Med 5d, Heavy 20d, Critical+ every 30 min/5 min/min) — success drops a level, QR10 raises; worst-level penalty until healed/treated.

**Exhaustion** (fatigue, mana, etc.): hard exertion → EN/WP check, fail = **+1 level**. **Full** penalty to its own domain, **half** to all else, tracks **stack** (round half up). Clears by **rest, one level at a time** — depth 1 = breather, 2 = long break, 3 = sleep, 4 = near-coma, 5+ = intervention. 4+ converts to wounds.

**Power pools** (Mana/Piety/Spirit): gather roll → success = free · marginal/fail = +1 exhaustion · QR10 = fizzle + exhaustion. **Push it:** take a level for a one-off **+4**.

# ForeWord — Introduction & Definitions
<!--{ "parent": "foresight-1986", "order": 1 }-->

*ForeSight (1986), pp. 9–12 — machine-extracted, work in progress. [About this restoration](/foresight-1986/).*

<!-- 1986 p.9 -->

#### [1.0] ForeWord
Designer's Notes: ForeSight (abbreviated FS) was originally intended as a science-fiction based roleplaying game, but has been extended to a generic format. However, it is presented in these core rules as a science fiction game-system, rather than as a skeletal system.

In general, the rules are formatted as follows:
Designer's Notes: are comments by the designer of a general nature, regarding rationale, explanation, and so forth; Definitions: are of (commonly used) game terms and objects; Procedures: are explanations of game mechanics in terms of quantities and objects defined in the game rules. ForeSight was designed with certain parameters in mind. These were the minimisation of problems common to many currently available role-playing games, namely:
(a) Perceivable differences between ·observed reality· and the ramifications of the game system, ie. falsehoods implied by the game-system, and truths denied by it. (Equally, I felt that between these extremes, likelihoods of given events should be plausible.)
(b) Interned inconsistency in fact, and of style and tone, within the rules themselves, combined with numerous situational special cases, ego games with a different rule to govern each skill.
(c) Poor rules grounding of non-combat actions by characters. In many games the only set of rules that a player can ·depend· on are the combat rules, which means that in a tight situation, these are the rules to which players often turn.
(d) Increasing complexity of games attempting to avoid the above. The design approach was straightforward: I took a very nice resolution system (the ease-factor - quality rating system from James Bond 007) and made it capable of dealing with more diverse circumstances than it had been able to, and in some cases more ·realistic·; I used this system for, more or less, everything (ie. combat or non-combat). In one step problems (a), (b), and (c) were minimized. In order to attack (d) I threw out and generalised as many rules as I COUld, and attempted to put every possible piece of information on the character sheet that I could, in as convenient a form as I could manage. Since then, the rules have been ironed out by fairly rigorous play-testing. Finally, I have attempted to make the rules as terse as possible: I seldom elaborate on special cases, although I am willing to reply to questions so long as no expense, or great trouble, on my part is involved; -Designer's Notes· were kept to a minimum, and the descriptions of many game objects were minimized if analogues are familiar to most people, or information on them is available in other places (eg. a good encyclopadia). Tonio Loewald (Canberra. 1987)

#### [1.1] Definitions
Definitions: The following are commonly used game terms and concepts, and are for convenience defined here in alphabetical order.

Ability: an ability in ForeSight is usually a skill or an attribute (if you think of knowledge as a sort of possession), and reflects some sort of capability (as one would expect).
Attributes: a character or creature in ForeSight (FS) has values for various things called attributes. These are quantifications of native, untrained abilities he/she/it possesses. References to a specific attribute possessed by a character are to his/her value for that attribute; to be specific, to hislher trained value in the attribute (which by default is set at the inherent value until improved or perhaps worsened). This value is a number, for humans it varies between five and sixteen. The Attributes in ForeSight are: ST (Strength): a character's ability to apply force with his/her body. EN (Endurance): a character's ability to continue expending energy without rest.

DX (Dexterity): a character's manual dexterity. AG (Agility): a character's balance, and bodily coordination. IN (Intelligence): a character's ability to reason. PC (Perception): the ability of a character to note changes and incongruities in his/her environment. WP (Willpower): a character's strength of Will, resistance to despair, ability to resist temptation, determination, etc.. EM (Empathy): a character's ability to relate to and understand others of his/her (and possibly another) species. AP (Appearance): a measure of the character's (sexual) attractiveness to others of his/her species.
Character Sheet: a player character's physical, mental, and emotional makeup, and his or her knowledge and capabilities, are recorded in gameterms on the Character Sheet, which is recognisable by having ·Character Name· written in its top left corner.
Character Worksheet: the more transient aspects of a character's existence are recorded on the Character Worksheet. A character's credit, possessions, fatigue, transit status, experience points, fields he/she is currently studying, weapons, armour, and so on, and so forth, should be recorded on this sheet. This sheet is separate since it will require more frequent replacement than the Character Sheet proper. This sheet is labelled ·Character Worksheet for ... •

e 101

<!-- 1986 p.10 -->

010.0100.06.05: represent dice. A 010 involves a ten-sided die. usually numbered 0.1 •..• 9; in FS read 0 as 10. so rolling a D10 yields a number from 1 to 10. A 0100 involves two ten-sided dice. differently coloured. which are called the tens and units die; one rolls them and reads them tens die first. but reading 00 as
100. so rolling a D100 yields a numberfrom 1 to 100. A 06 is a standard cube-shaped die. usually decorated with dots. and is used normally. A 05. used mostly in Star System Generation [7.0]. is obtained by rolling D10. halving the result. and rounding up any fractions.
Fields of Familiarity: these are more implicit than explicit in the game system. and are a quantHication of a character's general familiarity with some subset of the situations a skill might be applied in: ego A character with Ground Vehicles skill is assumed to be familiar with any vehicles in hislher possession at the start of an "adventure". but may not be familiar with some strange vehicle that he/she comes across in the course of hislher exploits. Most fields of familiarity are set at zero. and have no game effect; H negative. they reflect unfamiliarity. and have a detrimental effect; H positive (rare) they reflect long experience with the situation. and even a preference for it. Rules section
[2.4] deals with Fields of Familiarity.
Fields of Knowledge: in FS [character] capabilities are divided. roughly. into two sorts: skills and knowledge. Knowledge is something one has. or has not. whereas a skill is a continuously honed ability. Acquiring a Field of Knowledge requires a certain amount of time. which may be modified by previous attempts. and/or the character's inherent abilities (eg. an exceptional memory). In some sense knowledge in FS is not only possessed. but must to some extent be understood. by the character. When a character has completed his/her studies of a field. he/she rolls against a multiple of his/her IN (intelligence) attribute. In character generation this will either give or not give the character the field; in experience the character will gain the field of knowledge at some degree of familiarity. ie. the character will have the knowledge. but will not have it entirely clear in hislher mind how it all hangs together. See sections [2.3] Fields of Knowledge. and [2.5] Experience. A Field of Knowledge represents a broad grounding in the field named; some familiarity with all major concepts. and sufficient knowledge to know what detailed information to look uP. and where to find it GameMaster (GM): the gamemaster in FS is responsible for designing the imaginary setting for the game to take place in: the Game World (or Universe. in this case) as it were. He/she is also responsible for determining how the player characters and the setting interact (by setting I refer not only to geographical locale. but also to inhabitants. and whatever). In FS it is necessary for the GM to have a reasonable grasp of the rules. while the players need no such knowledge; she/he must also do a fair amount of work, or spend a fair amount of money, or both. On the other hand, GMs have more fun.

Gravity, Temperature, Environment Familiarity: FS. as a Science Fiction based Role-playing Game, deals not only with characters in a nice environment in which they have always lived, and which they intend to continue living in, but with a widely varying set of environments, most of them at least potentially hostile. The gravity modifier G appears in in the BEFs (base ease factors) of skills (or attributes, like Speed) dependent upon agility. an attribute representing balance, and accuracy of movement. In any given circumstance where a value for G is needed, the ambient gravity determines which modifier is used: in l T (light) gravity one uses the value under l T, ego 2. so a BEF might equal G+2. or 4. The gravity slots are NW (Near Weightless: 0 to 0.40 earth gravities), l T (light: 0.41 to 1.00), HY (Heavy: 1.01 to 1.60). and EX (Extreme: 1.61 to 2.50). Beyond that, no-one is really in any shape to argue (for E. E. "Doc" Smith based campaigns, multiply gravity values by ten). The temperature modifier T appears in BEFs of skills dependent on Willpower, since a person who is enduring a climate twenty degrees hotter than he/she is used to is hardly likely to be fit to resist physical pain on top of it. concentrate on a game of cards, or appear suave and charming. Whenever a value of T is required, use that appropriate to the character's ambient temperature. These modifiers assume adequate apparel. but not air conditioned space suits. The temperature slots are VC (Very Cold: -90 to -51 degrees Celsius), CO (Cold: -50 to -11 degrees Celsius), NL (Normal: -10 to 39 degrees Celsius), HO (Hot: 40 to 69 degrees Celsius), and VH (Very Hot: 70 to 89 degrees Celsius). In each slot is also a small number, this is the number of hours between a character's mandatory Fatigue checks. The Environment modifier E appears in BEFs of skills dependent on perception. since a good idea of what to expect in a place allows a person to concentrate on worthwhile subjects for his/her attention. Environment familiarities are expressed on a table to allow the great variety of possible environments to be compactly expressed. In general the environment is expressed as a contour (BR: broken, UN: uneven, FL: flat) and a surface feature (BN: barren, LV: light vegetation, MV: medium vegetation, HV: heavy vegetation. MA: marsh, IC: ice); there are also miscellaneous environments tacked onto the (in my opinion on the day) most appropriate places (S F: surface of water, S B: submerged in water. SU: suburban, ie. scattered buildings, UR: urban, ie. built up). Wherever a value for E is called for, the most appropriate is chosen.
Final Note: the GM determines which slots are most appropriate in all cases (the players, of course, can argue); If none seems appropriate, G, E, and/or T, have a default value of 2 (this fact is noted on the Character Sheet).
Inclination: while what a character can do is determined by hislher abilities, what he/she chooses to do is governed by his/her inclinations. A player character's inclinations are described under Personality Traits, on the bottom right of the character sheet

e 102

<!-- 1986 p.11 -->

NPC: a Non-Player Character is a game persona not controlled by any player, and hence usually controlled by the GM.
Permanent: some characters will have "permanent" backgrounds, meaning that their parents' occupations did not call for frequent changes of address. Examples of such occupations include teachers, GPs, and shopkeepers.
PC: a Player Character is a character whose actions are governed by one of the players in a game of ForeSight. While the player determines what the character wants to do, the GM often determines whether or not he/she successfully does it.
Role-Playing Game: a role-playing game involves players and a gamemaster. In a role-playing game the gamemaster (GM) creates an imaginary setting, and the players create (player) characters (PCs) who live in it. Play is generally fairly unstructured with the basic idea being that the GameMaster describes the current situation, and the players describe their character's actions within it; these are resolved, and then the GameMaster describes the new situation, and so forth. The role-playing comes into it when players try to have their characters perform actions which agree with their character's imaginary psyche, rather than with their own. A great deal more is said on the nature of roleplaying in the Designer's Commentary (at the back of the book). Roll, Task, Resolve: When some character in ForeSight attempts to do something, this thing is referred to as a task, often associated with some capability: ego climbing a mountain is a Climbing (skill) task, while figuring out what's wrong with a computer is a Diagnose (skill) / Computer/Robot Tech (Field of Knowledge) task. A Roll in ForeSight is the procedure by which the success of a task is evaluated, or, in other words, the method by which the GM may Resolve a task. Most rolls are performed at some modifier (eg. a lightly wounded character makes Pain Resistance rolls at -1). This modifier affects the Ease Factor (EF) of the roll. Positive modifiers make rolls more likely to succeed, while negative modifiers have the reverse effect. All of this is more fully explained in the Resolution rules (section [3.0]).
Skill: as opposed to a Field of Knowledge, a skill is a procedure with which a character has some degree of familiarity. A character in FS can learn the basics of a skill, reflected by gaining that skill at level one, and then proceed to hone it, with use or training, so that he/she gradually improves it. Some skills in FS function independently of any other capabilities possessed by the character, while others work in concert. Quite a lot of skills in FS involve the use of Fields of Knowledge in some way, and perhaps can handle seemingly incompatible Fields. The rules governing skills are covered in the skill rules ([2.2] Skills), and also sections [2.3] Fields of Knowledge; [2.4] Fields of Familiarity, and
[3.0] Resolution (which covers the resolution of tasks in FS).

SVU: the Standard Value Unit, abbreviated "svu" and pronounced "svoo", represents a measure of value and not currency, approximately equivalent to US$2.50 as of 1985 (about enough to buy a reasonable meal at McDonalds, if such a thing is possible). The svu is divided into one hundred centisvu (or "cents").
Transient: some characters will have "transient" backgrounds, meaning that their parents' occupations (or, perhaps, inclinations) called for frequent changes of address. Examples of such occupations include: fruitpickers, circuit court judges, and engineers.
Transit Status: I'll bet you're cussing me for not listing this under Current -. Tough. Transit status has no place in the Core Rules, since it is an aspect of my Science Fiction campaign, rather than a part of the essential rules, but it does illustrate how crime can be considerably reduced by simple mechanisms. Simply put: a character's transit status represents the Electronic Funds Transfer system to which hislher ID/credit account is attached, generally expressed as a planet, or nation. A character who is discovered outside the bounds of the system to which his/her account is attached is obviously there illegally (and he/she should expect at least some inconvenience - how much depending on how well he/she can convince the authorities). A character leaving one system for another has his/her account placed in transit, annotated with the prospective destination upon departure. If he/she reaches his/her stated destination, then his/her account is attached to the destination system. The master of a starship which habitually plies a route between two systems may apply for a dual attachment, allowing transaction in both systems. Finally, note that I am referring to EFT systems, not star systems here.

#### [1.2] Conventions
Designer's Notes: There are a few important conventions in ForeSight which will be stated below, as ever, for your convenience.
Rounding: unless otherwise stated, any decimal or fractional value which has to be converted into an integer for some game purpose (eg. PCSs can be fractional as calculated) is rounded off, ie.: to the nearest integer. Rounding up means treating any number between n-1 and n (n an integer) as n. Rounding down means treating any number between n-1 and n (n an integer) as n-1.
Page Numbering: the nth page of rules section m is numbered m hundred and n (so, for example, this is the third page of section 1.0 and is thus page 103).
Lack of Explanation: if I have decided (by some arbitrary and probably inaccurate process) that something is too obvious to warrant special explanation, or is something about which better information is available elsewhere, then there may be no explanation of it anywhere, and you'll have to use your common sense.
For example: Many skills are not explained, since explaining them would simply involve copying tracts from a dictionary or encyclopaedia.

e 103

<!-- 1986 p.12 -->

Most fields are unexplained. Unlike FASA, I do not pretend to be able to define an entire field of human knowledge in a few lines, and do not want to leave myself open to criticism by specialists. Some procedures call for a random QR (quality rating) to be used to determine some effect; in such a case roll D10 and consult the table below:

I

Random OR Table 010 Roll

OR

3-5

6-10

I

Some procedures can result in a tie, and do not explain how such an eventuality is dealt with: each of the tied results has an equal chance of prevailing. Eg. if in a three sided combat all three leaders obtained equal QRs and furthermore had equal Initiative PCSs (ie. they were tied), each would have an equal chance of obtaining the best initiative, and each of the two remaining would have an equal chance of coming second. Such events are rare. In general if people have found some concept difficult, or some rule poorly phrased, I have endeavoured to explain it in depth, or rephrase it, respectively.

[1.3] Technological Levels Each technological level (TL) represents a level of technological (and, to a lesser extent, social) achievement. (Later on, you will find a distinction between "soft" and "hard" technology. # Initiative
<!--{ "parent": "conflict", "order": 1 }-->

*One-pager. Initiative answers **when do you act — and who knows what, when?** It cuts a tense situation into brief rounds and orders who moves within one. It runs combat, but equally a quick-draw, an ambushed negotiation, a courtroom, a car chase. Its companion is [Intense Action](/intense-action/): Initiative sets the **when**, Intense Action prices the **how much**.*

Tense situations run in **rounds** — brief bursts separated by waiting for someone to make a move. A round is as long as the contest's tempo demands: direct combat is roughly 3–5 seconds with random lulls (ducked behind cover, catching your breath); a pursuit or a negotiation runs longer. Don't track the clock — the GM sets the tempo to fit the scene.

## Awareness: from narrative to "shit going down"

The hard, real moment is the transition out of story-telling into a fight. Every character enters it somewhere on a spectrum:

> **Surprised** (woken by the attack) → **Startled** → **Alert** → **Ready** → **Lying in wait** (the ambusher)

**Awareness and position drive Initiative.** Coarse, obvious effects modify it: a visored helmet or a blind corner is a disadvantage; a sniper studying the scene in safety, or the enemy behind you with the height, is a large advantage. Ballpark each from about **+4** (you see everything and they don't; you're behind them) to **−4** (the reverse). Need a number for awareness? It's about **½ (Perception + Stealth)**. Once the fight is live it tends to level out to one question — *can you see what's happening?*

## The round

1. **Roll Initiative** (awareness/position-driven). Order everyone best to worst; ties broken by Score.
2. **Declare, in order, act or wait.** Acting resolves when declared. Waiting holds for a trigger.
3. **Waiting persists.** Anyone still waiting from last round stays waiting until their declaration comes round again. *The totally unaware get no declaration on round one at all — which is why ambushes are murder.*

A **QR7** Initiative roll is **panic**: act all-out offensive *or* all-out defensive (go berserk, or run and hide) — no holding back. A **QR10** is a **freeze** — you lose the three seconds. It's only three seconds; they may be your last.

## Reaction & pre-emption

When a waiting character reacts to something (usually someone else acting), they may go **immediately after** it — or try to **pre-empt** and act **just before**:

> **Pre-emption = a Coordination roll, modified by your Initiative QR** (ties: Initiative Score). Reflexes do the work; awareness only biases the odds — no good having lightning reflexes if you're confused. Succeed → just before; fail → just after. It's still a roll, so even a superb, well-placed shooter keeps real uncertainty.

A pre-emption can itself be pre-empted (the counter-sniper), but you'll rarely go deeper. And **you never see each other's Initiative** — that uncertainty is the whole point.

> **You never know for certain you'll act first.** Pretty sure, never certain. The gunslinger *probably* draws first; the sniper *probably* fires before the hostage-taker reacts; neither is guaranteed. It's exactly why a police sniper in a standoff is loath to just shoot the other sniper — and why these scenes work here and collapse into "highest number wins" everywhere else.

*E.g. an archer waits — trigger: "the mage does something." The mage starts a spell; the archer pre-empts (QR of Initiative). On success the arrow lands before the spell goes off — but a confident archer can still be a hair too slow.*

## Beyond combat

This is **initiative for any tense situation** where timing and nerve decide the outcome, not only when weapons come out:

- **The quick-draw / Iai duel** — both waiting, each triggered by the other's move; pre-emption *is* the duel.
- **Business machinations** — who commits first, who holds a move in reserve, who read the room (awareness) before anyone spoke.
- **A legal battle** — objecting *just* before the answer lands; holding an argument for its moment.
- **A car chase** — see [Pursuit](/pursuit/): longer rounds, the same act-or-wait and pre-empt.

*Designer's Note: the experiments that drove this whole system were the Western shootout, the same shootout with a dastardly sniper, the Iai duel, and the hostage standoff. None of them resolve correctly in any other TTRPG — the nastiest edge cases of combat, which vastly more complex systems (Aftermath, I'm looking at you) never even tried to model. They cost one page here because the actor never *knows* they'll go first: every ruling is "make an Initiative roll and read its QR." Nothing to memorize, and the probability arrows all point the right way.*

# Introduction
<!--{ "parent": "core", "order": 1 }-->

ForeSight is a general-purpose role-playing game. It first appeared in 1986 as a science-fiction game system, grew a fantasy and historical sibling (*HindSight & the Age of Reason*, 1988), and was substantially rewritten in 2004. This edition is a streamlining of all of that: one book, one rule, and a character you can build in five minutes.

*Designer's Note: this edition bears a very strong resemblance to a game that was typed on twenty sheets of paper in 1984–85. That's probably the result of one very good design decision: ForeSight has one rule for resolution. Nearly everything else has been simplified, consolidated, or deleted — usually by noticing that two rules were secretly the same rule, and keeping the better one.*

## What ForeSight Is

**ForeSight is about more than just combat.** A lot of role-playing games are little more than combat systems with some arm-waving to cover all other forms of human activity. ForeSight's resolution rule applies to everything — picking a lock, charming a border guard, performing surgery, shooting someone — so the rules players can depend on in a tight spot are the same rules they use everywhere else.

**ForeSight runs lean and mean.** Combat happens quickly — minutes, not hours — partly because the resolution system is easy to use from memory, and partly because weapons are lethal.

**ForeSight is plausible.** The game was designed to minimize falsehoods implied by the game system, and truths denied by it. Likelihoods of events should be believable. Ordinary people are representable, not just adventurers. Looks matter, knowledge matters, and nobody becomes an expert scuba diver by winning a Nobel prize.

**ForeSight is transparent.** Game systems should not color the underlying setting. ForeSight is adaptable *to* settings rather than grafted *onto* them: the same rules have run hard SF, swords-and-sorcery, espionage, and the Age of Reason without changing anything but the equipment lists and the available talents.

**ForeSight is the rules you can remember.** When game mechanics are used, it should be easy to apply them, and the rulebook should seldom — if ever — need to be opened at the table.

The design philosophy behind all of this is simple: **keep the mechanics simple, push the probabilities in the right general direction with the right general magnitude, and let the results speak for themselves.** ForeSight doesn't try to simulate reality precisely; it tries to make believable things likely and absurd things rare, using rules you can run from memory. Time and again that produces lifelike outcomes nobody had to write a special rule for — and that's the whole idea.

## What You Need

At least one player willing to be the gamemaster (GM), one or more other players, two ten-sided dice per person (ideally in two colors, to roll D100), copies of the character sheet, pencils, and an adventure or the makings of one.

## Darn Good Reason

Every rule in a role-playing game will be broken at some point, and many will be broken frequently. A player or GM who wants to stretch, break, or ignore a rule should give a Darn Good Reason.

That's it.

## How To Use This Book

Rather than memorizing the rules, get the gist of them. A player needs the next chapter (the One Rule) and a character — the chapter after that shows how to build one in minutes. A GM should be thoroughly familiar with Resolution and passingly familiar with the balance of the text. ForeSight is not a game for rules-lawyers — although, with them in mind, ambiguities have been minimized — but a role-playing game best played with all the rules you can remember.

*Designer's Note: if you have never played a role-playing game before: a role-playing game involves players and a gamemaster. The GM creates an imaginary setting; the players create characters who live in it. The GM describes the situation, the players say what their characters do, the outcomes are determined (usually by common sense, sometimes by the One Rule), and the GM describes the new situation. The role-playing comes in when players have their characters act according to their characters' natures rather than their own. The GM does more work, but GMs have more fun.*

#### [2.0] Characters
Designer's Notes: the character is the most important object in a role-playing setting; like a television program or a motion picture, a role-playing adventure generally deals with the interactions of central characters (the protagonists - in this case the player characters) and their environment, including not only natural hazards and dire beasts, but other (perhaps non-human) characters (the supporting caste of allies, antagonists, and bystanders - the non-player characters). The rules in this section deal with the creation of both player and non-player characters.

#### [2.1] Character Generation
Designer's Notes: The Player Character (or PC) is the most important product of a role-playing system. The following rules enable you to generate a (human) character for the FS system cold, ie. without any knowledge of the other rules. Of course knowledge of the other rules helps.
Procedure: A PC in FS is generated using the following procedure. A copy of the FS character sheet is necessary.

#### [2.4] Fields of Familiarity
Procedure: a Field of Familiarity is a number (usually negative) reflecting the degree of familiarity a character has with a particular situation or item. A character is assumed to be familiar with any thing he/she possesses at the beginning of an "Adventure", and with any situation he/she has previously dealt with. When faced with a new situation or item to/with which a character wishes to apply a skill, the GM decides how foreign the situation or item is the the character and assigns an N FM (non-familiarity modifier, also referred to as familiarity) to it: -3 for very strange, to -1 for somewhat similar to something the character is familiar (ie. has familiarity zero or better) with. When in doubt, make the NFM -2.

There are three ways of improving an NFM: during play, a character may grow more familiar with a situation or item, and this is reflected by improving it by one (but never above zero), every time the character achieves a QR 1 or 2 in a task involving the situation or item; after a session where a character has been assigned an NFM, that NFM is removed, assuming the character is able to continue contact with the situation or item; experience may provide positive familiarity with a situation or item with which the character has been familiar with for over a year (see Experience, directly below). Note that these last rules apply to familiarity with situations and items, not fields of knowledge. NFMs for fields of knowledge are handled differently in that they cannot be improved by die rolls, but only by expending experience points, see [2.5], [3.0]. Players may wish to record their familiarity with things in the space provided. Recording familiarity with possessions and the like is unnecessary, as it is assumed; but situations are less obvious. Examples of situations and items requiring application of NFMs: a character must use a strange Aircar to make an escape, since the controls are unusual, but not entirely unfamiliar, an NFM -1 is assigned, which is nullified once the character achieves his/her first OR 1 or 2, or finishes the adventure and can study the machine at leisure; a character brought up in modem society lands on Darkover and is unused to strange and implicitly different social conventions, which can easily result in hislher causing considerable offense, the GM assigns an NFM -3 to the society, applying to all interactions (seduction, confidence, charisma, especially) and perhaps social studies, and so forth again this can be ameliorated by good ORs, or out of game-time experimentation - but note that familiarity with Darkovan society in this case reflects figuring out how to avoid offending people, not an understanding of the society, which would be a field of knowledge on its own.

#### [2.5] Experience
Procedure: in most role-playing games there is some method by which a character's abilities may improve as a result of the training and experience obtained by that character. In ForeSight a character may be improved by expending experience points (as distinct from generation points). A character gains experience points by being played, the number thus gained depending on the duration and quality of play of the owning player.

The basic award of experience in FS is 75 experience points (or EPa) per four or five hour session of play per character. This amount may be modified at the GM's discretion along the following lines: competent, productive play should receive higher awards, but not more than an extra 25 bar in exceptional circumstances, while a similar amount should be deducted for incompetent, unproductive play. Similarly adjustments for superior and inferior role-play should be made, on the basis of whether the character's actions befitted hislher stated persona. The upshot of this is that a character will receive 25 to 125 experience points per five or so hours of play. ~i::·····"""·······"·"··· ·"·"·""· ·· ···"····'···· "·'··

i Current Studies_ ii

A character receives any experience points due him/her only when the GM feels that the "adventure" the character is currently involved in has drawn to a close, or at least a sufficient respite from the action is available to him/her. There are certain limitations placed upon the expenditure of EPs based on this delineation of adventures; a continuous, and less arbitrary system is in the works for ForeScene. Experience points may not be transferred between characters, of course. Also see Teaching skill under Skills [2.2].

Expending Experience Points The following are methods of expending experience points to improve abilities. If a time requirement in days is stated, then four hours out of each (sidereal) day are required; any monetary requirement is subject to negotiation with the GM (and his/her NPCs) and other PCs if necessary. Acquire Skill at level 1: Exp (of skill) x 5 EPs, 14 days, instructor required (probably Exp (of skill) x 500 SVU cost); Exp (of skill) x 7 EPs, 28 days, appropriate references (Exp (of skill) x 100 SVU); Exp (of skill) x 10 EPs, 56 days.

<!-- 1986 p.24 -->

Raise Skill Level from n-1 to n (may only be performed once per skill "between adventures"): Exp (of skill) x n EPs. Raise Temperature or Gravity Familiarity from n-1 to n (must have dwelt in such climes recently, and may only be performed once "between adventures"): n"2 x 5 EPs. Raise Environment Familiarity from n-1 to n (must have dwelt in such climes recently, and may only be performed once per familiarity "between adventures"): n"2 x 2 EPs. Raise Trained Attribute Value from n-1 to n: n x 20 EPs, 28 days. Raise NFM (may only be performed once per field "between adventures"): from -3 to -2, 2 EPs; from -2 to
-1, 10 EPs; from -1 to 0, 20 EPs. Acquire Long Term Familiarity With Item (allows a character to treat one item which he/she has been using for at least one year as though it has a PM one better than before (eg. +1 becomes +2). A character may at most possess a number of such items equal to his/her IN): 40 EPs. Acquiring Fields of Knowledge As well as improving the skills and familiarities of their characters, players will also wish to expand the fields of knowledge possessed by their characters, ie. gain fields of knowledge in addition to those acquired in character generation [2.11. For a character to acquire a field of knowledge he/she need expend no experience points, but must instead devote about four hours per day for the time specified for that field (adjusted, perhaps, if the character has an exceptional memory, or has previously failed to acquire the field being studied); a character may thus go about his/her normal business while studying no more than one field. At the end of the stipulated time the player owning the character makes an IN roll at the EF listed for the field. The OR of the roll determines whether or not the character has successfully gained that Field of Knowledge and also the NFM (non-familiarity modifier) associated with that field for the character. The NFM is, assuming success, that listed for the field (a negative number) + 1 if a OR 2 was achieved, + 2 if a OR 1 was achieved (but not if it makes the NFM positive, in which case raise it to zero). A OR 7 indicates failure, but decreases the time required to acquire the field subsequently to half the normal time; while a OR 10 indicates nothing has been learnt, and does not affect subsequent attempts to acquire the field. Note that this procedure does not correspond to that 'in character generation, and it is not recommended that it be used there.

Unlike NFMs for situations or items (Fields of Familiarity
[2.4]), these modifiers may only be improved by experience point expenditure (see [2.5]), since entire fields of knowledge are considerably more complex than individual situations or items. If a character wishes to use a field he/she has not finished studying (but has at least half completed), or has previously failed, the GM should assign a modifier equal to the field's NFM - (half the number of years required to learn the skill); Do not adjust this number for memory, etc.. Time spent in boring circumstances, ego on spacecraft, should count double towards time spent studying fields, while time spent adventuring, and so forth, should not count at all. A character who takes time off to study should be able to learn one field twice as quickly (perhaps only if he/she makes a WP roll) or two fields concurrently.

#### [2.6] Fatigue
Designer's Notes: Although fatigue is a skill in FS it is treated differently to other skills, in some respects. As well having a pes, a character has fatigue values: a character's Threshold Fatigue is a reflection of a character's ability to bounce back from exhaustion (if you want to be technical, the character's body's ability to convert over to glycogen-glucose consumption); the formula for this is on the character sheet, and its value should be filled in. A character's Reserve Fatigue measures his/her overall fitness, and training, and equals the sum of his/her threshold fatigue, and fatigue skill level. Finally, a character has a number of Fatigue Points (recorded under fatigue on the reverse side of the character sheet) equal to his/her fatigue PCS, this value is also referred to as Normal Fatigue.

Climatic Adversity makes a character tired. In the top right hand corner of the box under each temperature bracket on a character sheet is a number (call it t). Combat is tiring: every Mov., Evad., Mel •• Attack, Opportunity Attack, Parry, or Dodge action costs half of one fatigue point to perform. There are ways of regaining fatigue. A character's fatigue cannot drop below zero, and if one of the procedures above calls for such a drop, then fatigue is reduced to zero instead. A character on zero fatigue suffers a -2 modifier to all task resolution attempts, UCDC, and to hislher speed. A character who has been reduced to zero fatigue since he/she last slept, but is not at zero fatigue, still incurs a -1 modifier to all task resolution attempts, UCDC, and to speed. [2.7] Psionics Psionics in FS are presented for those who wish to use them, not as an integral part of the implied GameWorld, but as a module which can be added to it painlessly. H you want to make psionics integral to the Game-World, either give them to everybody in some degree (eg. make them available to everybody, exactly like normal skills), or tie them to communications, faster than light travel, or some other all-pervasive aspect of the environment. Normally, a player character has a psionic skill if and only if it is so indicated under abilities and limitations. The GM may discuss with the player which ones he/she can have, or send word down from the mountain. The Exp value of skills reflects the cost to improve them, not to acquire them. In some places psionic characters are persecuted by society (especially if it can detect them), so players may eliminate them by paying the cost for removing any other ability or limitation. A psionic task succeeds or fails normally, but using a psionic skill always costs the- psionic character fatigue equal to the OR of the attempt, and if a OR 10 was achieved, increases hislher wound level by one. H this cost exceeds the character's remaining fatigue, then the character automatically fails, and has hislher fatigue reduced to zero, or may take the excess fatigue loss as an increase in wound status, and die after the task is completed; a character can (deliberately) die this way. Usually, the results of psionic tasks have a base duration, which determines how long the effects of the skill's application last. This duration may be doubled by expending additional fatigue equal to that lost in the attempt, tripled by spending twice that much, and so forth; but may not increase the duration to more than thirty times normal (this is a limitation on characters killing themselves, really). Where applicable, tasks with targets more than 10km away suffer a -1 penalty, more than 100km away a further -1, etc., so that a task which affects a target 15000km away, suffers a net -4 penalty.

[2.8] Non-Player Characters A non-player character (NPC) is a character not controlled by a player. ie .• in most cases. a character controlled by the GM. Such characters. by nature. will be far more numerous than player characters. while the GM is far less numerous than the players. This means more work for the GM. who already has to figure out how the entire Universe worksl The solution is simple: [i) Do not generate important NPCs the way PCs are generated. If this wasn't already obvious. the best way to generate an NPC is decide what attributes. skills. etc. such a character would possess. and give them to him/her. Finished. Don't bother about experience points· for NPCs either. If they survive, and the PCs bump into them again, maybe they've gotten better at sometl:ling, maybe they've been too busy.

<!-- 1986 p.27 -->

[ii] Wing it. If the situation calls for a plumber, then he/she's probably pretty reasonable at plumbing (Diagnose PCS-15; Repair PCS-20; knows Construction). If he/she has to do anything else, then he/she's probably poor to fair at it (no skill, to PCS.10, say). Just remember the following: a PCS of 10 is not particularly good; PCS-15 is okay; PCS-20 is pretty good; and PCS-25 or better represents expertise. Most NPCs will not engage in physical labour (a lot of plumbing will be done by robots, I expect, these are covered in ForeScene), and will have low Pain Resistance and Fatigue (say 10), similarly they will avoid combat (again say 10), while they will have average capacities for other common skills (Empathy, Search, Scan, and perhaps some vehicle at 15). If an NPC does something for a living, give him/her 20, or perhaps 25, in it. Simple. Do not use these guidelines for all NPCs, just the vast majority.
Also: the stats of most NPCs, especially minor ones, are generally irrelevant, and generic values can be assumed. A number of generic NPCs are supplied for your convenience, each simply requires appropriate fields of knowledge. [iii] NPCs are not as good as PCs, at least in general. Certainly powerful villains whom the PCs have sought long and hard, should be more than a match for a solitary PC, or at least possessed of wicked henchpersons, but by and large, NPCs, having less initiative, and drive, than PCs, will possess lesser capabilities. Bear this in mind. If an NPC is to be generated, the way a PC is, then give himlher base values of 3 in all attributes except AP (which remains 5). Otherwise generate the character as per normal (roll 06+2 rather than 06+4 if the semirandom method is desired). This system may be used by players who wish to generate their characters' spouses, siblings, etc. (subject to GM intervention: "Why does your husband have such a high Handguns skill, while you claim he works as a pharmacist?"). Apart from that, less space should be required to list an NPC's capabilities than a PC's, so a (more compact) NPC record is provided.

[2.91 Merits, Demerits, and Notoriety (Optional) If a character works for somebody, or is involved in some form of pecking order, then it is a good idea for the GM to keep some numerical record of hislher situation. In ForeSight a character's status in a hierarchy can be kept track of via merit points (MPs, if you like abbreviations). When a character is seen to perform some (contextually) meritorious act, he/she will gain merit points, and if he/she is seen to perform some unmeritorious act, he or she will lose merit points (or gain demerits). Note that inaction may, in some cases, constitute either a meritorious or (more probably) an unmeritorious one.

Example: a character who is a law enforcement officer might gain MPs for preventing an armed hold-up, successfully resolving a hostage situation, or rescuing a drowning person from a river; he/she might lose MPs for not attempting to do any of the above in appropriate circumstances, or displaying incompetefICS or poor judgement in an attempt to do one of the above, or using unconventional and unsanctioned methods to do any of the above (especially if he/she fails). Merit points are in general non-transferable: one's MPs gained as a policeman count for nothing if one becomes a spaceship pilot, but some proportion of one's merit points might be convertable to a related field: a paramedic might retain half of his/her merit points if he/she became a fire-fighter (and if he/she returned to being a paramedic, he/she could have the higher of hislher previous merit as a paramedic, and half hislher merit as a fire-fighter). Merit points may accord a character benefits in terms of position and promotion, salary, choice of assignment, privileges, respect, medals, and/or trust (placed in himlher by hislher employer, and/or colleagues).

An act within the line of duty, but beyond normal expectations, should be accorded 1 to 5 merit points. Eg. a policeman is expected to deal with a small scale hostage situation, but to resolve it without casualties or major mobilisation would be worth merit points. An act within the line of duty, but beyond any expectation, should be accorded 6 to 20 merit points. Situations of this sort would occur most often when unforeseen events cause a character's superiors to knowingly allocate insufficient resources to a task, and the task is successfully performed anyway; and when there is more to an assignement than first appeared. Eg. a squad is assigned to seize an ·undefended" village which turns out to be defended by a platoon of veteran troops, and nevertheless prevails; or a mathematics student sits a first year exam in which hislher lecturers have placed a "Great Unsolved Problem· as a joke, and he/she solves it without realising the joke.

Notoriety Notoriety is a special case of MPs. A character gains notoriety for being believed (by law-enforcement agencies, the mass media, and/or the public) to have performed criminal acts. A character loses notoriety points for serving the prison sentences, or whatever, accorded to people who commit the crimes the character is seen to have perpitrated. Each point of notoriety is roughly equal to a year's imprisonment in today's terms, although how this works out will vary from place to place (eg. some places today put people in prison longer for harmless sexual eccentricity than for violent rape). A given crime will accord notoriety points (NPs if you prefer) to the character suspected of having performed it roughly equal in number to the number of years of imprisonment a person today would expect to serve if tried for a similar offence in some contemporary western nation. Eg. 20 NPs for second degree murder, 5-10 NPs for armed robbery, 0.1 NPs for parkingltraffic violations. A crime whose NP total is less than one twentieth of a character's existing notoriety will not contribute to hislher notoriety (eg. a character with notoriety ~2 no longer acquires notoriety for parking violations). A character's notoriety rank (see above) determines who is after himlher, and how badly they want himlher, and also, perhaps, the size of the reward for information leading to his/her arrest. Role-playing a character in a prison is likely to be pretty dull (unless, for some reason, the authorities allow him/her to roam free on some "prison planet"). The above are examples, of course, and may not apply in specific instances, but I expect you get the idea.

# Intense Action
<!--{ "parent": "conflict", "order": 2 }-->

*One-pager. Intense Action answers **how much can you do at once, and how well?** It replaces the action-point and "how many actions" bookkeeping that thrashed between every past edition with one idea: **attention is finite, and your modifier is how you spread it.** Its companion is [Initiative](/initiative/) — Initiative sets **when** you act; this sets **how much**.*

There is no action budget to track. In a round you have one **primary** focus, room for one deliberate **secondary** action, and your **automatic / reflex** actions — dodging, flinching, keeping balance, noticing — ticking along underneath. What you *can* do is set by the body and by skill, not a point pool; what it *costs* is attention.

## Your modifier is how you spread your attention

**Split your focus and everything suffers.** Declare your deliberate tasks in priority order:

| You are attempting | 1st | 2nd | 3rd |
|---|:--:|:--:|:--:|
| **one thing** | 0 | | |
| **two things** | −1 | −2 | |
| **three things** | −2 | −3 | −4 |

Each task takes −1 for every *other* task, and −1 more for each task ranked above it. Take the hit as an **ease factor** (you do it worse) or as **effectiveness** (you do less of it) — a divided move covers **a third to a half** the ground rather than failing outright. Read one column, as always: worse *or* less.

**Concentrate — go all-in on one thing — and buy a bonus at your reflexes' expense.** Pour everything into a single task and it gains a **positive** modifier (about +1; more for absolute tunnel-vision), but your **automatic / reflex actions take a penalty**: you won't notice the flanker, you won't dodge well. The sniper who lives inside the scope makes the shot and is oblivious to all else. That trade *is* the choice.

**Promote a reflex when you want it done well.** Automatic actions happen on their own at a baseline; spend real attention on one and it climbs — **+1 as a secondary, +2 as your primary** (measured against leaving it automatic). *A sniper watching for a target: make noticing his **primary** and it's +2 to spot; keep the shot primary but really want to see and it's +1.*

**A secondary action cannot pre-empt.** You can't win the race to act (see Initiative) with something you're only half-attending to — pre-emption belongs to your primary.

## How many beats do you get?

The ladder above is how *well* each thing goes; this is how *many*. A statement of intent unfolds as beats — draw · aim · fire, or lunge · wind-up · blow (see [Fire](/fire-combat/) and [Melee](/melee-combat/) combat) — and **your Score in the ability sets how many fit in a round**:

> **Beats in a round: your Score ÷ 5 as your *primary* ability, ÷ 10 as a *secondary* or tertiary one — round up.**

Skill *is* speed and facility: the gunfighter cycles and fires faster, the swordsman lands more strikes. This is "how much" set by the body and by skill — not an action-point budget with a price list. And being secondary costs you twice over: half the beats *and* the ladder's penalty on each.

*Firearms 25 (a 20+1 shooter), all-in: 25 ÷ 5 = **5** — Aim · Shoot · Aim · Shoot · Shoot. Melee 18 on the attack: 18 ÷ 5 → **4** — stab · stab · wind-up · stab; with defence as his secondary, 18 ÷ 10 → **2** — block · block.*

**An attribute used as the ability counts double.** Movement is Coordination, a shove is Strength — and a raw attribute tops out about where a trained skill is just getting started, so it would otherwise buy almost no beats: **double it for this**. In a firefight you're usually *moving and shooting* — Firearms primary (the shots), Coordination secondary (the footwork). Coordination 8 doubles to 16 → 16 ÷ 10 → **2** movement beats: *pop up · [shoot] · hide*. The lumbering CO-5 bruiser doubles to 10 → just **1**: he can pop up or drop back down, not both as an afterthought, so he's caught in the open — unless he makes *moving* his primary (10 ÷ 5 → 2) and takes the shot as a ragged secondary.

## What counts as a task

**A task is a thing you want *rolled*.** That is the whole test, and it polices itself. A step, a shouted word, drawing a weapon, aiming — these aren't tasks; they happen, with honest consequences (pop up to fire and you're still half-exposed when the round ends). There are no "free actions": a thing is either of no consequence, or it isn't free. But it only costs you *attention* if you cared enough to roll for it. So *advance–attack–retreat* is one task — the attack — and takes no penalty. Decline to make your movement a task and you simply move: noisily, visibly, at the GM's discretion.

## Help sheds tasks

A helper doesn't hand you a bonus — they **take a task off your list**, and the ladder does the rest. A sniper ranging his own shot *and* firing is two things (the shot at −1); give him a spotter who owns the ranging and he's down to one, at 0 — the spotter is worth exactly **+1**, and it falls out of the rule. Two consequences worth having: help can't push you past your own focused best (the ladder bottoms out at one task, so assistance can't be stacked into absurdity), and a helper who takes nothing gives nothing — the shed task is real, the spotter rolls it, and a spotter who blows the roll hands over bad numbers. A helper who is genuinely *better* than you is a separate thing — good information — earning an ordinary situational bonus (the *aimed* / *braced* family), not a rung on this ladder.

## Reactions: parry, dodge, flinch, duck

Reactions are tasks too — but ones you *didn't plan*, so they're priced apart. Not a pool: take as many as you like, each at a **cumulative −2**. Keep parrying and you simply get worse at it; skill decides how far down that ladder you stay dangerous — so the better fighter gets more good reactions, with no bookkeeping.

> **The parry you saw coming is cheaper than the parry you didn't.** Tasks you *declare together* share the ladder above; a reaction you were surprised into pays the full −2 each. This is a large part of why waiting — declaring a trigger and holding for it — is worth so much.

- **Parry** (opposed): a critical parry lets you counter; an overwhelming one leaves the attacker off-balance (disarm, or trade places).
- **Dodge** (opposed): **dodge and give ground** for a one-off advantage — which is what makes melee *move*, fighters circling and yielding ground instead of standing toe-to-toe.
- **Flinch / duck:** exposed and shot at, ducking back to cover is a legitimate reaction (at the stacking penalty).

## Never pay twice

The ladder prices dividing *your own* attention. **The situation's ease factor prices the world** — range, cover, light, the target's movement — never your multitasking. If firing-on-the-move already cost −1 for being two tasks, it does *not* also take a separate "firing on the move" penalty. Charge it once, on the ladder, and leave it there.

## Beyond combat

Attention is finite everywhere. A **Pursuit** is this at a longer tempo — driving *and* shooting *and* reading the road split the same way. **Space combat** is a crew *shedding tasks* to one another (that is what a crew is *for*), each station one focused task. And because the split is measured against the round, the rule scales with tempo for free: move-and-watch are two tasks inside a three-second firefight, one-each across an afternoon of tracking.

*Emergent tactics: in almost every other RPG, players concentrate fire to kill one target at a time, because a dead enemy is the only less-dangerous enemy. In ForeSight a wound is −(level) to everything and a stun takes an enemy out of the turn, so a hurt, rattled foe is dramatically less dangerous than a healthy one. Once the worst threats are handled, the smart play is to **spread** attacks across as many enemies as possible — degrade the whole group rather than execute one at a time. It falls out of the rules on its own, and it mirrors how real firefights are won: by suppression, not by headcount.*
